newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Separatist Georgian region holds presidential poll.
newsitem.headline: Separatist Georgian region holds presidential poll.

text.p: Georgia's separatist region of South Ossetia voted in a presidential election on Sunday which the Georgian government says is a setback to peace moves after a bloody conflict.
Voting began at 0900 (0400 GMT) in Tskhinvali, capital of the sparsely-populated region which declared independence from Georgia in 1990 and was at war from 1991 to 1992.
The South Ossetian Central Elections Commission expected 80 percent of the 40,000 registered voters to turn out to choose between four candidates.
Current leader Lyudvig Chibirov was expected to face a stiff challenge for the newly-created post from "prime minister" Vladislav Gabarayev.

Chubirov, a 64-year old ethnographer who is formally Chairman of Parliament, has led the rugged mountainous region since 1993 and engineered moves to find a peaceful settlement with the Georgian government.

South Ossetia, a chunk of territory about the size of Luxembourg, declared independence as the Soviet Union was disintegrating and Georgia was gripped by a wave of nationalism which minority groups feared.
Clashes between ethnic Ossetians, an ancient Caucasus ethnic group which speaks a language related to Persian, and local Georgians turned into war in 1991.

Late Georgian nationalist President Zviad Gamsakhurdia sent in armed forces in an unsuccessful attempt to crush the independence drive. Fighting with Ossetian volunteers killed more than 1,000 people and left thousands more homeless.
Most Georgians have fled the region but several thousand still live in scattered villages where the election is not being held.

South Ossetia's entreaties to Moscow to be allowed to annex itself to Russia have generally fallen on deaf ears. Many Ossetians want to join their ethnic brethren in Russia's neighbouring region of North Ossetia.
Although Chibirov still pays lip service to independence, economic woes, crime and the realisation that no country is about to recognise South Ossetia have led him to seek compromises with Tbilisi.
This culminated in the signing of a preliminary political accord earlier this year.
The Georgian government has criticised the holding of the vote, saying it could damage the peace process.
The other candidates have also advocated continued negotiations with Georgia but some observers say that Chibirov's opponents could take a harder line in talks.
